solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Foreign banker keeping money for building material?

indicators.note: one thing keeping another holds it within, so the letter goes inside the river's name

parts.note: the Tiber is a river in Italy, and a river is a 'banker' in crosswords because it has banks

explanation.surface: An overseas bank official holds on to funds meant for construction supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreign banker' looks like a financier abroad; it is a river outside Britain, the Tiber.
explanation.definitionFit: Wood cut and prepared for carpentry is the classic stuff builders use; the question mark admits it is one example.

clue.text: Normal look lacking gravity in a manner of speaking

parts.note: par is the normal or standard level, as in golf or 'feeling below par'

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so a letter is dropped from the word for a look

parts.note: a glance is a quick look
G is the physics symbol for gravity

explanation.surface: An ordinary glance, without weight, is in a manner of speaking what's described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a manner of speaking' is an idiom on the surface, but 'in' is only the link and 'manner of speaking' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Parlance is a particular way of using words, a style of talk or jargon, as in 'legal parlance'.

clue.text: Why a biker's treated marginally

indicators.note: treated means processed or worked on, so these letters are rearranged into new order

explanation.surface: Someone asks why a motorcyclist has been dealt with only slightly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treated' shuffles the ten letters of WHY A BIKER'S, the apostrophe ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: To win by a whisker is to win by the narrowest gap, so the phrase means only just, by a tiny edge.

clue.text: Principal place supplying water

definitions.meaning: a water ... is the large pipe carrying the supply; poetically the ... is also the open sea

explanation.definitionFit: The word works as the adjective for chief and as the noun for the principal pipe carrying a town's supply.

clue.text: Term actor devised around Italy for an opponent of cronyism?

indicators.note: around means the shuffled letters are placed on both sides of the country code
devised means invented or made up anew, so the letters of the two words are recast

parts.note: I is the international vehicle registration code for Italy

explanation.surface: A performer coins a word, set in Italy, for someone against favouring friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devised' rearranges TERM ACTOR to MERTOCRAT, and 'around' puts that round I.
explanation.definitionFit: A believer in rule by merit would oppose jobs handed to friends, hence the question mark for a definition by example.

clue.text: Quantity of fish in college dining room, it's said

indicators.note: it's said means the word is spoken, so we want something that sounds the same but is spelt differently

parts.note: in British colleges the hall is the communal dining room

explanation.surface: A catch of fish being served in a college's dining room, reportedly.
explanation.walkthrough: In Oxford and Cambridge colleges, 'Hall' is the dining room where meals are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: A haul is the catch landed from one cast of a net, so a quantity of fish taken.

clue.text: Role not right in Australian film

indicators.note: not here means without, so the letter for right is left out of the word for a role

parts.note: a part is a role in a play

explanation.surface: A part, without a correct actor, in an Australian movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'film' looks like a movie in the surface, but it means a thin coating.
explanation.definitionFit: A patina is a thin surface layer, like the green sheen on old bronze or gloss on aged wood.

clue.text: Ordinary writer, US one, devouring dry dish

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level
the writer of the clue refers to themself as me

indicators.note: devouring means swallowing, so the first group of letters goes round the abbreviation for dry

parts.note: a US writer: Harper Lee, author of To Kill a Mockingbird
TT means teetotal, so dry in the sense of not drinking alcohol

explanation.surface: An everyday author and an American one tuck into a dry meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Crossword setters call themselves 'me'; 'US one' extends 'writer' to the American novelist Harper Lee. TT, teetotal, is the usual crossword sense of dry.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaten eggs fried in a pan and folded make a simple savoury plate of food.

clue.text: Where one might find travel items, whatever happens

definitions.text: Where one might find travel items
definitions.meaning: travel items such as clothes are packed in some suitcase or other

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for regardless, while read literally it says the luggage is inside some bag.

clue.text: Fear internalised by international army

indicators.note: internalised by means held inside these words, so the letters are found within them

explanation.surface: A fear held privately by a multinational fighting force.
explanation.definitionFit: Alarm is sudden fright or anxious apprehension at a danger.

clue.text: Obvious triumph for a former PM

definitions.note: Stanley Baldwin was British Prime Minister three times between 1923 and 1937

parts.note: bald means plain or obvious, as in a bald statement
a win is a triumph or victory

explanation.surface: A clear victory for an ex-prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Baldwin led Conservative governments in the 1920s and 1930s, so he is one past head of the British government.

clue.text: Shunning outsiders, silly prince in a familiar way creates hostility

indicators.note: shunning outsiders means the first and last letters of silly are dropped, leaving the inner ones

parts.note: Will is the familiar short name of Prince William

explanation.surface: A daft prince who avoids strangers in a chummy manner causes bad feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'creates' is a link word between the wordplay and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill will is animosity or malice felt towards someone, a set phrase for antagonism.

clue.text: Destruction with island disappearing in series

indicators.note: disappearing means the letter for island vanishes from the word for destruction

parts.note: ruin is destruction or devastation

explanation.surface: Destruction comes as an island vanishes in a sequence of events.
explanation.definitionFit: A run is an unbroken sequence, as in a run of wins or a print run.

clue.text: Cheerful daughter in a hot region for recreation

indicators.note: in here means placed inside, so the abbreviation for daughter goes within the rearranged letters
recreation read as re-creation means making again, so these letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A happy daughter visiting a warm area for leisure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for recreation' looks like a holiday, but read as re-creation it remakes A HOT REGION; 'in' puts D inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in good heart is an idiom for being in high spirits, optimistic and well.

clue.text: A large number consuming eg gin in rough form might show this?

definitions.text: A large number consuming eg gin in rough form might show this?

indicators.note: consuming means swallowing up, so the shuffled letters go inside the word for a large number

parts.note: a gross is a large number, twelve dozen or 144

indicators.note: in rough form means in a crude, disordered state, so the letters of eg gin are rearranged

explanation.surface: Many people knocking back gin and the like might end up unsteady.
explanation.walkthrough: A gross is twelve dozen. Read as a whole, the clue also pictures a crowd of drinkers feeling the effects, so wordplay and definition are one.
explanation.definitionFit: Grogginess is dazed, unsteady weakness, as after too much drink, so heavy gin drinking might bring it on.

clue.text: Husband with spring flower first stuck indoors?

indicators.note: first means the river name comes ahead of the word for spring

parts.note: a flower in crosswords is something that flows, a river; the Ouse is an English river
to bound is to spring or leap

explanation.surface: A husband, with a spring bloom first, is confined to the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' looks like a bloom but is read as 'one that flows', a river: the Ouse is a river in England.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone housebound cannot leave home, usually through illness or age, so they are stuck inside.

clue.text: Stop on road, we hear, to get rest

indicators.note: we hear means as spoken, so a word that sounds the same but is spelt differently

parts.note: to brake is to stop a vehicle on the road

explanation.surface: A driver pulls over on the road, it seems, to take a breather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A break is a pause or interval for relaxation, as in a tea break.

clue.text: Sybil's partner is known initially as one with a fearsome look

parts.note: in the British sitcom Fawlty Towers, Basil Fawlty is the husband of Sybil

indicators.note: initially means only the opening letter of known is used

explanation.surface: Sybil's other half is, at first, known for a fierce stare.
explanation.walkthrough: Fawlty Towers is a 1970s BBC sitcom about the hotelier Basil Fawlty and his wife Sybil.
explanation.definitionFit: The basilisk is a mythical serpent whose gaze could kill, so its stare is deadly frightening.

clue.text: A stroke has this other acute risk in initial stages

indicators.note: in initial stages means the first letters of the following words are taken

explanation.surface: A medical stroke brings another serious danger in its early stages.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about a medical stroke; in rowing, the stroke is the oarsman who sets the pace, and holds one.
explanation.definitionFit: In a rowing crew the stroke is the rower nearest the stern, and each rower pulls a blade.

clue.text: Posh grandee's first to enter enclosure? That's the custom

parts.note: U means upper class

indicators.note: to enter means to go inside, so the letter goes within the enclosure

parts.note: an SAE, a stamped addressed envelope, is something enclosed with a letter

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of grandee is used

explanation.surface: An upper-class nobleman leads the way into a paddock as is the tradition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enclosure' suggests a fenced area, but it is an SAE, a stamped addressed envelope sent with a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage is established practice or habit, especially in the way language is used.

clue.text: Scrape in a bar so after an exchange

indicators.note: after an exchange means once the letters have been swapped around, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cut gained in a pub after an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after an exchange' suggests a row of words; it rearranges IN A BAR SO.
explanation.definitionFit: An abrasion is a graze, where skin has been rubbed away.

clue.text: Female featuring in FT great use for stirring female campaigner

indicators.note: featuring in means appearing within, so the letter goes inside the rearranged letters
stirring means mixing up, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A woman appears in the Financial Times, great for rousing a campaigner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link word; 'stirring' rearranges FT GREAT USE.
explanation.definitionFit: Suffragettes were the early-20th-century British women who campaigned, often militantly, for the vote.

clue.text: Guard criminal missing old fellow

indicators.note: missing means without, so the two letters are removed from the word for a criminal

parts.note: an offender is a lawbreaker
O is old and F fellow, both standard abbreviations

explanation.surface: A security guard is a lawbreaker, without his old pal.
explanation.definitionFit: A fender is a guard, such as a low metal frame before a fire or a buffer on a boat.

clue.text: Artist close to boycotting tabloid

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, is the crossword's usual artist

indicators.note: close to means the end letter of boycotting is used

explanation.surface: A painter is nearly shunning a downmarket newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A rag is a scornful name for a cheap, sensational newspaper.

clue.text: Good field for those with titles?

parts.note: the field is the full set of entrants in a race, its entry

explanation.surface: A fine set of competitors in a title contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'those with titles' hints at sports champions; the gentry are titled landowners, though strictly ranked just below the nobility, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The gentry are the well-born, landowning class of people, many holding hereditary ranks or honours.

clue.text: A property owner in the French region's borders needs source of light

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so these letters go within the French article

parts.note: le is the French word for the
the National Trust is a British charity that owns stately homes and land

indicators.note: borders means only the outer letters of region are used

explanation.surface: A landlord in the French area needs a lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Trust (NT) is a British charity owning historic houses and countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: A lantern is a lamp in a protective case, so it gives out light.

clue.text: Peer cut short before due time

indicators.note: cut short means the last letter is chopped off the word for before time

parts.note: early means before the expected time

explanation.surface: A nobleman's visit ended prematurely.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is a British nobleman ranked between marquess and viscount, a member of the peerage.

clue.text: See American wearing good French loose-fitting jacket

indicators.note: wearing means having on, so these letters are clothed in the French word for good

parts.note: bon is French for good
lo is an old word for see or look

explanation.surface: An American shown dressed in a good French loose jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: A blouson is a short jacket gathered at the waist so it puffs out above.

clue.text: Booklet taken out at intervals for a speed merchant?

indicators.note: taken out at intervals means every other letter of booklet is chosen

explanation.surface: A pamphlet removed periodically for a fast salesman.
explanation.walkthrough: Usain Bolt, the Jamaican sprinter, is the speed merchant; the question mark marks a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Usain Bolt holds world records in the 100 and 200 metres, the fastest man in history.

clue.text: Use bad language in opening to summer sport

indicators.note: opening to means the first letter of summer is used

parts.note: to sport clothes is to wear them

explanation.surface: Someone curses at the start of a summer game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sport' looks like a game but is a verb, to wear proudly; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To swear is to curse or utter profanities.

clue.text: Duke is put in role spun to show a magnificent look

indicators.note: is put in means placed inside, so the letter for duke goes within the rearranged letters
to show signals that the letters of role spun are rearranged into a display

explanation.surface: A nobleman cast in a part that's been twisted to look grand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spun' reads as the anagram signal, but ROLE alone is too short: all eight letters of ROLE SPUN are rearranged, round D.
explanation.definitionFit: Splendour is grandeur or magnificence of appearance.
